cells.tense: You are here at the half-lit edge, deciding from what you already know.
cells.act: ask the question you do not know the answer to
cells.ask: Before your next call goes out, ask one question whose answer you genuinely don't have. Sit with it a beat, then move.
cells.core: Half-light suits this: you can decide hard and still notice what you don't know. You act from what you already hold, and it lands clean. You're not waiting on the whole road and not pretending to see it; you take the step that's showing and ask one honest question before making it. Your read on a situation turns out right because you let the question stand instead of closing it early. That quiet listening isn't a brake on the charge — it sharpens it. When the perception comes, it doesn't argue, and neither do the people near you. That's the balance worth feeding: charge and curiosity in the same breath, neither one muzzling the other. Before the word goes out, ask the thing you don't yet know, and hear what answers.
cells.sheetLine: You decide from what you know and still ask what you don't.
cells.verb: Charging forward into a call that has not finished forming
cells.place: Half-light, where only the next step is legible

cells.tense: You are bracing for a call that hasn't been handed to you yet, forcing the shape before it arrives.
cells.ask: Take a situation you're trying to force into shape. Write three moves you actually have. Stop there. Don't make them yet.
cells.core: You're running past the light that's showing. You need the call settled before it's formed, need the pattern in hand the moment the ground shifts. Boundaries go down hard and fast, before anyone — including you — knows what they're for. The charge is real; it's just arrived before the terrain does. Your mind does something finer than speed: it can think a thing through to its sharp point and get it exactly right. So use that on one situation rather than the next ten. See the shape of it before the foot moves. That's not hesitation — some decisions genuinely need the whole pattern seen first. Sharpen a single situation; let the others stay unshaped for now. What's under the push is surer than the push, and it'll still be there when the ground stops moving.

cells.tense: You stood at the edge a while, and the decision didn't come, and you turned from the door without marking it.
cells.act: move the structure one real inch
cells.ask: On anything undecided near you, do the smallest real thing that still has to be done. One inch. Then stop there.
cells.core: The step stopped coming. Nobody's been charged forward out of here in a while; the call that arrived hasn't been made. The room waits, and the waiting has stopped feeling like waiting. What's gone quiet isn't nerve — it's the steady work that used to carry the charge through. So put a hand on the structure and shift it an inch. Not a plan, not a decision, not a view of the road. The smallest real thing, done slowly. You don't have to feel like it. The doing starts what the waiting drained, and the next inch will show its own light once your hands are working again. A step taken is worth more here than a step chosen well.
cells.sheetLine: The step stopped coming because the steady effort stopped.

cells.tense: You are already writing the call, pen down, telling yourself you're only watching the room.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Pick something you've kept holding that's already finished. Set that down this week. Keep everything else as it is.
cells.core: The call is being made by you and the account of it doesn't include you. From your side you're just listening, just noticing which way things lean. Meanwhile the thing has moved, and it moved because you moved it. That's not a flaw; it's the shape of this work. What's also true is that something finished is still being held, and holding it is what makes the account feel like someone else's. Set one done thing down. Not the whole load — just that, actually released. The room won't applaud and doesn't need to; the weight lightens and the story can catch up. What's left after you let go will be more plainly yours, and the pen will be where it has been.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the seat is actually running on empty in Status 3 — the record calls it a mechanics: energy into the vertical twin pulls current through the starved seat, not that the person has withdrawn from leading. A reader could reasonably say: no, the reason I'm not deciding is that nobody's waiting on my call, not that I've abandoned the seat. The ask survives being wrong: forcing one inch of real change teaches something whether or not the read was right. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line that makes 'uncertainty' sound like a wound rather than terrain.
